questions.enonce_markdown:
Using the suggested annotations, translate the following arguments into symbols:
(i) Nothing good comes easy. (Gx: x is good; Ex: x is easy).
(ii) Not all countrymen painted the picture of the pope (Cx: x is a countryman: Px: x painted the picture of the pope.).
(iii) If anything is extravagant, then it is gullible. (Ex: x is extravagant; Gx: x is gullible).
(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** "Nothing good comes easy" means: for every thing $x$, if $x$ is good then $x$ is not easy.

$$(x)(Gx \supset \sim Ex)$$

(equivalent to $\sim(\exists x)(Gx \cdot Ex)$: there is nothing that is both good and easy).

**(ii)** "Not all countrymen painted the picture of the pope" denies the universal statement "all countrymen painted it".

$$\sim(x)(Cx \supset Px)$$

equivalent to $(\exists x)(Cx \cdot \sim Px)$: there is at least one countryman who did not paint the picture of the pope.

**(iii)** "If anything is extravagant, then it is gullible" is a universal conditional.

$$(x)(Ex \supset Gx)$$

(In (iii) the letter $E$ means "extravagant" and $G$ means "gullible", as annotated for that part; they differ from the meanings of $G$ and $E$ in (i).)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using the short truth table method, determine the validity of the following arguments:
(i) P ⊃ Q
    Q ⊃ R  /∴ P ⊃ R
(ii) ~A v B  /∴ P ⊃ R
(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The short truth table method tries to make the conclusion false and all the premises true. If this is impossible the argument is valid; if it can be done, the argument is invalid.

**(i)** $P \supset Q,\ Q \supset R\ \therefore\ P \supset R$

- Make the conclusion false: $P \supset R$ is false only if $P = T$ and $R = F$.
- Make the first premise true: $P \supset Q$ with $P = T$ requires $Q = T$.
- Then the second premise is $Q \supset R = T \supset F$, which is **false**.

The premises cannot all be true while the conclusion is false. The argument is **valid** (it is the hypothetical syllogism).

**(ii)** $\sim A \vee B\ \therefore\ P \supset R$ (as printed)

- Make the conclusion false: $P = T$, $R = F$.
- Make the premise true: $\sim A \vee B$ is true when, for example, $A = F$ (then $\sim A = T$), with $B$ either true or false. The letters $A$ and $B$ do not occur in the conclusion, so nothing prevents this.

| $A$ | $B$ | $P$ | $R$ | $\sim A \vee B$ | $P \supset R$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| F | F | T | F | T | F |

An assignment makes the premise true and the conclusion false. The argument is **invalid**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that p and q are True statements and r and s are False statements, determine the truth value of the following statements:
i) ~(q v p) v ~(~r . s)
(ii) [(r ⊃ p) ⊃ r] ⊃ s
(iii) ~(~p v s) . (r . s)
(3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Values: $p = T$, $q = T$, $r = F$, $s = F$.

**(i)** $\sim(q \vee p) \vee \sim(\sim r \cdot s)$

- $q \vee p = T \vee T = T$, so $\sim(q \vee p) = F$.
- $\sim r = T$; $\sim r \cdot s = T \cdot F = F$; so $\sim(\sim r \cdot s) = T$.
- $F \vee T = T$.

**The statement is true.**

**(ii)** $[(r \supset p) \supset r] \supset s$

- $r \supset p = F \supset T = T$.
- $(r \supset p) \supset r = T \supset F = F$.
- $F \supset s = F \supset F = T$.

**The statement is true.**

**(iii)** $\sim(\sim p \vee s) \cdot (r \cdot s)$

- $\sim p = F$; $\sim p \vee s = F \vee F = F$; so $\sim(\sim p \vee s) = T$.
- $r \cdot s = F \cdot F = F$.
- $T \cdot F = F$.

**The statement is false.**

**Answer:** (i) true; (ii) true; (iii) false.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Symbolise and determine the validity of the following argument using a truth table.
If farmers work hard, then they shall never suffer hunger, and the human society will not suffer malnutrition problems if the government assists the farmers with farm inputs.
(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Symbolisation.** Let $F$ = farmers work hard; $H$ = farmers suffer hunger; $G$ = the government assists the farmers with farm inputs; $M$ = the human society suffers malnutrition problems.

The two clauses ("If farmers work hard, then they shall never suffer hunger" and "the human society will not suffer malnutrition problems if the government assists the farmers with farm inputs") are joined by "and":

$$(F \supset \sim H) \cdot (G \supset \sim M)$$

**Truth table** (16 rows for four letters):

| $F$ | $H$ | $G$ | $M$ | $\sim H$ | $\sim M$ | $F \supset \sim H$ | $G \supset \sim M$ | $(F \supset \sim H) \cdot (G \supset \sim M)$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | T | F | F | F | F | F |
| T | T | T | F | F | T | F | T | F |
| T | T | F | T | F | F | F | T | F |
| T | T | F | F | F | T | F | T | F |
| T | F | T | T | T | F | T | F | F |
| T | F | T | F | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T | F | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T | T | T | T | T |
| F | T | T | T | F | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | T | T | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | F | F | T | T | T |
| F | T | F | F | F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T | F | T | F | F |
| F | F | T | F | T | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | T | T | F | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | T | T | T | T | T |

**Validity.** The final column contains both T and F: the statement is true in 9 rows and false in 7 rows, so it is **contingent**. It is not a tautology and no row can be called a logical necessity: the statement is **not logically valid** (it is true only on condition that the facts, hard work and government assistance, really lead to the stated results).

*If the passage is read as an argument* with the first clause as premise and the second as conclusion, $F \supset \sim H\ \therefore\ G \supset \sim M$, the same table shows it is **invalid**: the row $F = T$, $H = F$, $G = T$, $M = T$ makes the premise true ($T \supset T$) and the conclusion false ($T \supset F$). The two clauses share no letter, so neither can support the other. Under either reading, the answer is that it is not valid.
